recordNote: FishBase lists a largest published weight of 12.2 kg; a 14 kg fish from the Marié River was submitted as a world record.
description: The fish Barcelos is famous for: a long, heavy-shouldered cichlid that hunts the edges of the archipelago's lagoons and sandy banks. Young fish are speckled with pale spots; big ones turn gold with three dark bars and a black eyespot on the tail. It hits a lure like a falling tree and then tries to pull the angler into the timber.
facts: Adults hold in the deeper edges of lagoons and on the sandy and rocky banks of the main river.
It eats mostly small fish, especially characins under 10 cm.
The Barcelos region on the Rio Negro is known for world-record peacock bass.
visualNotes: Elongate, deep-shouldered cichlid; three broad dark vertical bars; black ocellus ringed in gold on the tail base; red eye; young fish and some adults spotted with pale dots; breeding fish golden-yellow with a hump on the head.

facts: It is usually caught in shallow water near the shore of lagoons and in slow reaches of the river.
Three large ringed eyespots on the flank give it its English name.

facts: Juveniles eat shrimp; adults are almost entirely fish-eaters.
It breeds three or four times a year rather than in one season.
Large breeding males grow a fatty hump on the forehead and defend a territory.

Oscars hang under floating plants and in mud-bottomed backwaters, taking small fish, worms and shrimp. In the Amazon it is a prized food fish long before it is an aquarium one.
facts: Both parents clean a spawning site and guard a clutch that often numbers in the thousands.
It is a highly esteemed food fish in South America.

The parents take the larvae into their mouths, and care can last six weeks.

It turns up in the main channel, lakes, tributaries and on the beaches alike.

Males guard the nest after the eggs hatch.
Live fish are hard and dangerous to handle because of the teeth and jaws.

description: A long, ribbon-finned surface hunter found only in the Rio Negro basin. It cruises just under the surface along flooded margins, watching the branches above with eyes set high on its head, and leaps clean out of the water to take beetles and spiders off the leaves.
facts: It is endemic to the Rio Negro basin.
The male carries the eggs in its mouth.
visualNotes: Very long, compressed body tapering to a small tail; dorsal and anal fins long and set far back, almost meeting the tail; upturned mouth with two chin barbels; young fish black with a yellow stripe, adults dark grey-blue with gold-edged scales.

description: The black arowana's silver cousin, found across the Amazon: long, armoured in big pearly scales and almost always at the surface. It can tolerate water low in oxygen, eats fish and insects, and is famous for jumping two metres out of the river to snatch prey from overhanging branches.
facts: It jumps out of the water to take large insects such as beetles.
The male carries the eggs, larvae and young in his mouth for nearly six weeks.
It can tolerate water low in oxygen.
visualNotes: Very long, compressed silver body with huge pearly scales tinged pink or blue; upturned mouth with two forward-pointing chin barbels; long dorsal and anal fins far back; small tail.

description: One of the largest freshwater fish on Earth: a long, armoured air-breather whose scales turn red towards the tail. Every few minutes it rises with a gulp that can be heard across a lake. As the river rises it moves out into the flooded forest; when the water falls it returns to the lakes.
facts: It must breathe air, and its gulp at the surface carries a long way.
It spawns in April and May, in a nest on a sandy bottom, and guards the eggs and young.
It moves into the flooded forest with the rising water and back to the lakes at low water.
visualNotes: Huge, elongate, cylindrical body; flat bony head with an upturned mouth; large thick scales, grey-green at the front and edged deep red towards the tail; dorsal and anal fins set far back near the rounded tail.

description: A massive catfish with a dark back, a pale belly sharply divided from it, and a tail the colour of a sunset. It hunts the bottom of deep pools and channels for fish and crabs and will eat fallen fruit too. Hooking one is easy; moving one is not.
facts: Adults eat fish, crabs and fruit.
It is potamodromous: it migrates within rivers.
visualNotes: Broad, flattened head with a bony shield and long barbels; dark grey-brown back sharply separated from a white-yellow belly band; bright orange-red tail and tip of the dorsal fin.

description: The giant catfish of the main channel: grey, broad-headed and long-whiskered, a long-distance migrant that hunts other fish on the soft bottom of deep water. Fishermen tell stories of piraíba big enough to swallow a monkey, and the stomach contents say they are not all exaggerating.
facts: It feeds on fish, and stomachs have been found to contain parts of monkeys.
It is one of the largest fish of the Rio Negro basin and a long-distance migrant.
visualNotes: Huge, elongate catfish; broad flat head; very long maxillary barbels; grey to dark brown back, pale belly; forked tail with long upper lobe; juveniles spotted.

description: A long, shovel-nosed catfish striped and spotted like a tiger, one of the most handsome fish in the river. It hunts small fish at night along the bottom of channels and lagoon mouths and is highly prized at the table.
facts: It was formerly treated as Pseudoplatystoma fasciatum in the Amazon.
Its maximum recorded length is 140 cm TL.
visualNotes: Elongate, cylindrical catfish with a long flattened shovel-shaped head; grey-brown back with dark vertical bars and spots, white belly; long barbels; forked tail spotted black.

description: A sleek, silver-grey catfish of the main channel with flat, ribbon-like barbels and a long, low fin along its back. It travels in schools over the bottom and bites best at night, when the fishing boats anchor on the deep bends.
facts: It occurs in schools and feeds on bottom-living animals.
Its barbels are flattened like ribbons, which gives it its Portuguese name.
visualNotes: Elongate, silver-grey catfish; flattened, ribbon-like maxillary barbels reaching past the dorsal fin; long, low adipose fin; deeply forked tail.

description: A squat, enormously heavy catfish with a broad flat head and mottled yellow-brown skin, living in the deep holes and muddy beds of the big tributaries. It hunts other fish at night and sometimes follows the migrating schools into flooded areas. It fights by refusing to leave the bottom.
facts: It is mainly a fish-eater that hunts at night, sometimes moving into flood-prone areas.
Fish of 130 cm and 50 kg are not rare.
It matures only on reaching about 10 kg.
visualNotes: Massive, short-bodied catfish with a very broad flat head and small eyes; yellowish to olive-brown skin with darker marbling; short barbels; rounded fins.

description: A round, brown freshwater ray covered in orange eyespots ringed with black, lying half-buried on sandy beaches and shallows. It is the reason Amazon guides shuffle their feet when they wade: the barbed spine on its tail delivers one of the most painful wounds in the river.
facts: Its tail spine causes painful wounds; FishBase classes it as traumatogenic.
It is the freshwater stingray most often imported by the aquarium trade.
visualNotes: Round, flat disc; brown above with many orange-yellow spots ringed in black; short tail with a serrated spine; pale underside.

description: Not an eel but a knifefish: a long, dark, round-bodied fish that breathes air and lives in the still, muddy margins of the lowland floodplain. Most of its body is an electric organ that can stun prey and warn off anything that bothers it. Anglers usually meet one by accident and remember it.
facts: Its high-voltage discharges range from about 151 V in a 20 cm fish to 572 V in a 61 cm fish.
It must breathe air.
It was described in 2019, when the electric eel was split into three species; this is the lowland one.
visualNotes: Very long, cylindrical, scaleless body; dark grey to olive above, orange-red throat and belly; flat head with small eyes; no dorsal fin, a long anal fin running almost the whole length of the body.

description: A fish no longer than a thumbnail, with an electric blue-green stripe above a scarlet belly. Shoals of them hang in the dark water of forest streams. Barcelos is built on them: the piabeiros of the middle Rio Negro catch them by hand-net for the world's aquariums.
facts: Most cardinal tetras in the aquarium trade are caught in tributaries of the Rio Negro and Orinoco.
It lives in shoals in the middle layers of acid blackwater (pH 4 to 6).
Barcelos calls itself the capital of the ornamental fish, with an annual ornamental-fish festival since 1994.
visualNotes: Tiny, slender tetra; iridescent neon blue-green stripe from eye to adipose fin; entire lower body bright red from snout to tail; translucent fins.

description: A small, translucent prawn of forest streams and leaf litter, with long thin claws and a habit of backing into the shadows. It is one of the few crustaceans that thrive in acid blackwater, and every fish in the igarapé knows it as food.
facts: It lives in small first-order streams, far from the coast.
Males reach about 2 cm in carapace length.
visualNotes: Small, slender, translucent brownish prawn with darker bands; long rostrum; second pair of legs as long, slender claws, longer in males.

description: The pink dolphin of the Amazon: a long-beaked, round-headed river dolphin that turns from grey to pink with age. Its neck bends, and it can steer slowly between the trunks of the flooded forest. It surfaces with a heavy breath every minute or two and is never far from the boats at Barcelos.
facts: Its neck vertebrae are not fused, so it can turn its head and manoeuvre through flooded forest.
Males reach 2.55 m and can weigh 185 kg; females are smaller.
Brazil banned fishing for piracatinga catfish because river dolphins were being killed for bait.
visualNotes: Long narrow beak with stiff hairs; bulging forehead; low ridge instead of a dorsal fin; large paddle-like flippers; grey when young, pink in adults, especially males.

description: A small grey dolphin of the main channels, shaped much like its ocean relatives and quite unlike the boto. Tucuxi travel in tight groups, chase fish in fast dashes near the surface, and leap and somersault where the river is wide. They are shy of boats.
facts: It lives only in fresh water, in the Amazon basin.
Groups chase fish together in quick dashes near the surface.
visualNotes: Small, streamlined dolphin; short beak; triangular, slightly hooked dorsal fin; grey to blue-grey back, paler sides and belly.

conservation.note: Endangered (IUCN). Hunted almost to extinction for its fur in the twentieth century.

description: The river wolf: a long, dark-brown otter as big as a man, living in noisy family groups that fish the lagoons and backwaters together. Each has a pale throat patch as individual as a fingerprint. A family that has caught a large fish lets the whole lagoon hear about it.
facts: Family groups usually have three to eight members.
It eats almost nothing but fish, especially characins and catfish.
Males reach about 1.7 m from head to tail and weigh up to 32 kg.
visualNotes: Very long, sleek dark-brown body; broad flattened tail like a paddle; webbed feet; cream throat patch with an individual pattern; round head with small ears.

description: The smallest of the Amazon river turtles, a blackwater specialist with bright red markings on its head. It lives in the flooded forest and quiet blackwater streams of the Rio Negro and basks on logs at low water. The middle Rio Negro holds one of its largest populations.
facts: The Rio Negro basin is the centre of its range.
It is the smallest Podocnemis: females reach about 32 cm in carapace length, males about 24 cm.
It prefers blackwater streams and flooded forest to the main river.
visualNotes: Small, smooth, dark brown-black oval shell; head dark with bright red or orange-red patches and stripes, brightest in juveniles and males.
